title: Flipping an Image
description: Brute force to optimized: reversing then inverting in two separate passes versus fusing both into a single two-pointer swap-and-invert step.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement
Given a binary matrix image, flip each row of it horizontally (reverse the order of elements), then invert it (every 0 becomes a 1, and every 1 becomes a 0). Return the resulting image.

blocks.caption: Two pointers swap and invert symmetric pairs in a single combined step

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","A binary matrix image (every cell is 0 or 1)"],["Output","The image after horizontally flipping (reversing) every row, then inverting every value"],["Goal","Produce the result in a single pass per row, rather than two entirely separate passes"],["Constraints","n == image.length == image[i].length; 1 <= n <= 20; image[i][j] is 0 or 1"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["A row needs to be REVERSED","A two-pointer swap from both ends moving inward, the classic in-place reversal technique"],["Every value ALSO needs to be INVERTED (0 <-> 1)","The inversion can be folded directly into the same swap step, avoiding a separate pass"],["Reversing a symmetric pair of positions naturally pairs two values together","Combine \"swap\" and \"invert\" into a single operation per pair, rather than reversing first and inverting second"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem
Given a binary matrix, reverse each row's order of elements, then flip every 0 to a 1 and every 1 to a 0, returning the resulting matrix.

blocks.title: Analogy: Mirroring and Color-Swapping a Row of Light Switches at Once
blocks.text: Like having a row of on/off light switches, and needing to both mirror their left-right order AND flip every switch's state, in a single pass. Rather than mirroring the whole row first and then walking through it again to flip every switch, each symmetric pair of switches can be handled together: take their two values, invert both, then place them in swapped positions, all in one motion.

blocks.caption: A symmetric pair is swapped and inverted together; a lone middle cell just gets inverted

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Row [1,1,0]: reversed is [0,1,1], inverted is [1,0,0]","Result row: [1,0,0]","Reversing then inverting (or equivalently, inverting-while-swapping) produces this row"],["Row [1,0,1]: reversed is [1,0,1], inverted is [0,1,0]","Result row: [0,1,0]","This row happens to be a palindrome before inverting"],["Row [0,0,0]: reversed is [0,0,0], inverted is [1,1,1]","Result row: [1,1,1]","Reversing an all-zero row changes nothing; inverting flips every value"],["Answer","[[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[1,1,1]]","Every row has been flipped and inverted"]]}

blocks.text: Edge case: a row with an odd length

When a row has an odd number of elements, its exact middle element stays in the same position after reversal (since it's equidistant from both ends), so it only ever needs to be inverted, never swapped with anything.
5. How Should We Think?
Before reversing an entire row first and then inverting it in a completely separate pass, notice that both operations can be combined into a single pass using two pointers.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: Reversing a row is classically done with two pointers starting at both ends, swapping the elements at those positions and moving inward until they meet.

Observation 2: Inverting a value (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0) can be expressed directly as (1 - value), a simple O(1) formula.

Observation 3: Since reversal already brings together a symmetric pair of positions at each step, the swap and the inversion of BOTH values in that pair can happen simultaneously: row[left] becomes (1 - the OLD row[right]), and row[right] becomes (1 - the OLD row[left]).

Observation 4: If the row has an odd length, the two pointers will eventually land on the same middle position; that lone element only ever needs inverting, since reversal alone would leave it exactly where it is.

Recognizing that "reverse, then invert" can be fused into a single "swap-and-invert" step per symmetric pair avoids ever needing two separate full passes over each row.
This is a two-pointer in-place technique, fusing the classic array-reversal pattern with a simple O(1) value transformation applied to both elements of each swapped pair simultaneously.
6. Brute Force Solution
Reverse each row completely first, then apply the inversion as an entirely separate second pass.
Step by step algorithm

items: For every row, first reverse its elements completely, producing an intermediate reversed row.
Then, in a separate pass over that reversed row, invert every value (0 becomes 1, 1 becomes 0).

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The reversal and inversion are kept as two entirely separate steps, since this brute force does not yet combine them.
An intermediate reversedRow array is materialized fully before the inversion pass begins.
result accumulates each fully processed row independently.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force
Every row is correctly reversed and then inverted, so the final result is always accurate.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * m), visiting every cell twice (once to reverse, once to invert), where n is the number of rows and m the row length.
Space: O(n * m) for the output matrix (plus a temporary reversed row per row, if not done in-place).

Limitation: performing reversal and inversion as two entirely separate passes over each row does twice the necessary traversal work, when both operations can be fused into a single pass using the same two-pointer positions.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force reverses each row fully, then inverts it in a separate pass. Instead, use two pointers (left and right) starting at both ends of the row. At each step, compute the inverted values of BOTH positions and place them in swapped order: row[left] gets (1 - old row[right]), and row[right] gets (1 - old row[left])), then move both pointers inward. If the pointers meet at a single middle position (odd-length row), simply invert that one value.

For each row, initialize left = 0 and right = row.length - 1. While left < right, compute the inverted value of the current row[right] to place at row[left], and the inverted value of the current row[left] to place at row[right], swapping them in a single step; then advance both pointers inward. If left == right at the end, invert that single middle element directly.
9. Optimized Solution
Use two pointers per row, swapping and inverting each symmetric pair in a single combined step.
Dry run for row = [1,0,1]

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","left, right","Action","Row after this step"],"rows":[["1","left=0, right=2","temp = 1 - row[0] = 1 - 1 = 0; row[0] = 1 - row[2] = 1 - 1 = 0; row[2] = temp = 0","[0, 0, 0]"],["2","left=1, right=1 (met)","Middle element: row[1] = 1 - row[1] = 1 - 0 = 1","[0, 1, 0]"]]}

blocks.title: Final result
blocks.text: The row [1,0,1] becomes [0,1,0], matching the expected result for this row (reverse it, [1,0,1] again since it's a palindrome, then invert every value).

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * m), visiting every cell exactly once (each symmetric pair is processed together in one step).
Space: O(1) extra if modifying the image in place (O(n*m) only if the output must be a separate new matrix).
Why This Works

Reversing a row is equivalent to placing the original row[right] at position left and the original row[left] at position right, for every symmetric pair; inverting is simply applying (1 - value) to whatever ends up at each position. Combining both means: place (1 - old row[right]) at left and (1 - old row[left]) at right, which is exactly the swap-and-invert step performed here, achieving both operations' combined effect without ever materializing an intermediate reversed-only row.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["left < right","Swap the two positions' values while inverting both simultaneously, then move both pointers inward"],["left == right (row has odd length)","The single middle element needs only inversion, since reversal alone leaves it in place"]]}

blocks.text: Code walkthrough

items: A temporary variable holds one inverted value before the other assignment overwrites row[left], preventing the original value from being lost mid-swap.
The loop condition left < right naturally stops before or exactly at the middle, handling both even- and odd-length rows correctly.
The final if (left == right) check handles the odd-length row's single unpaired middle element as a special, simpler case.

blocks.text: 10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space","Notes"],"rows":[["Brute force (reverse fully, then invert separately)","O(n * m)","O(n * m)","Each row is traversed twice: once to reverse, once to invert"],["Optimized (two-pointer swap-and-invert combined)","O(n * m)","O(1) extra (in-place)","Each row is traversed once, with reversal and inversion fused into a single step per pair"]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

When two operations both need to touch the same positions (here, reversal and inversion both touch every array position), they can often be fused into a single combined pass, rather than performed as two entirely separate traversals.
Common mistakes

items: Forgetting to use a temporary variable when combining the swap and inversion, which can cause one value to be overwritten before it's used to compute the other.
Handling the odd-length middle element incorrectly (either forgetting to invert it, or incorrectly trying to "swap" it with itself).
Reversing first into a genuinely separate array and then inverting, missing the opportunity to fuse both operations into one pass.

blocks.text: Interview tips

items: Point out explicitly that reversal and inversion can be fused into one pass using the same two-pointer structure, since recognizing this fusion opportunity (rather than just implementing the two steps separately) is what distinguishes a well-optimized solution here.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Reverse AND transform every element" (two operations touching the same positions) points toward fusing both into a single two-pointer pass, rather than performing them as two separate full traversals.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you handle a matrix where rows have different lengths (a jagged array)? The exact same two-pointer technique applies independently to each row, since each row's reversal and inversion are entirely self-contained.

What if the values weren't binary (0/1), but instead needed some other pairwise transformation combined with reversal? The same fusion technique generalizes: compute the transformed value from the OTHER position's original value, rather than assuming a specific (1 - value) formula.

Could this be done without any extra space at all, even for the output? Yes, by modifying the input image directly in place (as the optimized solution here already does), since no auxiliary array is required beyond a single temporary variable per swap.

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: The classic two-pointer in-place array reversal technique, extended here by fusing in an additional O(1) value transformation at each swapped position, a pattern reusable whenever reversal is combined with any other per-element operation.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * m) time, O(n * m) space.
Optimized (two-pointer swap-and-invert): O(n * m) time, O(1) extra space (in-place).
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: Two-pointer in-place reversal, fused with an O(1) value inversion at each swapped position
Core Idea: Reversal and inversion both touch the same symmetric position pairs, so they can be combined into a single swap-and-invert step per pair
Time: O(n * m)
Space: O(1) extra (in-place)
Most Important Observation: Two operations touching the same array positions can often be fused into a single pass, rather than performed as separate full traversals
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: row[left], row[right] = 1-row[right], 1-row[left]; invert a lone middle element directly
